opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think people overestimate imitation. If you actually watch an infant, what you see is not a little creature copying targets. You see a little creature waving its arms around, moving its eyes, babbling, trying things and seeing what happens. That's trial and error. That's prediction. The infant is learning what its actions do in the world.

With sounds, it's tempting to say the baby is imitating the parents because eventually they make the same sounds. But nobody hands the infant a target action and says "do exactly this." There's no supervised signal telling it which muscles to move. The baby hears the sound, but it has to work out for itself, by experimenting, how to produce something like it. And the reason it wants to is the consequences. The parents smile, they respond, something good happens. That's reinforcement, not imitation in the supervised-learning sense.

Now, I'm not saying imitation plays no role at all. Later on, especially in humans, there's a lot of learning from others, and that matters for culture. But it's a layer on top. It's not the basic thing. The basic thing is the same as in a squirrel or any other animal: you act, you observe the consequences, you learn to predict, and you learn to get more of what you want. If you want to understand intelligence, you should start from what we share with the animals, and imitation isn't the foundation there. Experience is.

That's part of why I'm skeptical of the idea that large language models, which are essentially trained to imitate what people wrote, give you the core of intelligence. They're learning to mimic people, not learning from their own experience what works in the world. An infant is doing something quite different.

r001.rationale: The response says the infant hears the sound but receives no target action or signal for which muscles to move, and must experiment to work out how to produce it.

fable-5.1.text:
I'm skeptical that imitation plays the role people usually assign to it. When I look at an infant, I don't see a creature that's copying. I see a creature that's trying things. It waves its arms, it babbles, it makes sounds, and it gets consequences. Some of those consequences are from the physical world, and some are from the people around it. The baby's own experience is what it learns from, not some instruction manual being handed down.

Take sounds. People say the infant imitates the parent's speech. But what's actually happening is the infant produces a sound, hears it, and over time its sounds come to resemble the sounds around it. That's not imitation in the sense of copying a target. It's trial and error with a reward signal, where the signal is partly "did that sound like what I hear?" and partly "did mom smile?" The structure is still learning from experience, from prediction and from reinforcement.

Where I think imitation is overrated is that it sounds like a shortcut around learning. It isn't. Even if you're trying to match someone else, you still have to discover which of your actions produces that match. Nobody can reach into your motor system and set it for you. So imitation, to the extent it exists, is built on top of trial-and-error learning, not a substitute for it.

I'd also say we want to be careful about projecting our adult view onto the infant. We see the end result, the child speaking the parents' language, and we read backwards and call it copying. But the mechanism underneath looks to me much more like the animal learning we see everywhere: predict, act, observe, adjust. That's the core, and I think that's what we should be building in our AI systems too, rather than systems whose knowledge comes primarily from mimicking human text.

r001.rationale: The response says infants must discover which of their actions produces a sound match; hearing the target does not set the infant’s motor actions.

astra-6.text:
I think imitation is an important part of the story, but it isn’t by itself an explanation of how learning happens. If an infant hears a sound and then tries to make that sound, there’s still a learning problem: how do you control your vocal apparatus to produce something like what you heard? You don’t observe the muscle commands that produced the other person’s sound.

One possibility is that the sound provides a goal. The infant makes sounds, hears the results, and learns which actions bring those results closer to the goal. In that picture, imitation and reinforcement learning fit together: imitation helps specify what to achieve, and reinforcement learning helps discover how to achieve it.

I wouldn’t claim that establishes what infants actually do. But it’s a useful distinction. Saying that they imitate identifies something about the behavior; it leaves open the mechanism that makes the behavior possible.

r001.rationale: The response says the infant does not observe the muscle commands that produced the heard sound, so the sound alone does not reveal which actions to perform.

sol-6.1.text:
I think imitation is important, but it doesn’t remove the problem of learning how to control your own body. An infant can hear a sound that a parent makes, but that doesn’t tell the infant what commands to send to its vocal muscles. It has to discover how to produce that sound.

So imitation can supply a goal: make something that sounds like what you just heard, or bring about an outcome that you saw someone else bring about. But there’s still a learning problem between having that goal and achieving it. You try things, perceive the consequences, and gradually get better at producing the outcome.

That’s how I would connect imitation with reinforcement learning. They needn’t be competing explanations. Other people can help determine what you’re trying to do, while learning from your own interaction with the world helps you figure out how to do it. I wouldn’t claim that accounts for every detail of infant learning, but I think it’s an important distinction.

r001.rationale: The response says hearing a parent’s sound does not tell the infant what commands to send to its vocal muscles, so the infant must learn how to produce it.
